OPEC’s fifty years bought it 1.5 per cent a year
Kieślowski’s sci­en­tist fa­ther, his skat­ing son, and a les­son in hu­mil­ity

brief.head: Monopoly needs a state
brief.text: Cartels can­not last where any­one is free to enter a mar­ket, Amit Varma said. Lasting mo­nop­o­lies exist only where[[x3]] the state hands some­one an ad­van­tage. {004-C01}

brief.head: Armies aren’t for home
brief.text: The mil­i­tary is built to mar­shal un­be­liev­able lev­els of vi­o­lence, Ajay Shah said. Its train­ing, man­u­als and tac­tics are not wisely ap­plied to India’s own peo­ple. {004-C10}

brief.head: Kyiv taken, war lost
brief.text: Even had Russia taken Kyiv, Amit Varma ar­gued, it could never have won the coun­terin­sur­gency that fol­lowed. Ajay Shah said that had been his base­line from the start. {004-C13}

brief.head: Battleships of state
brief.text: Big Indian in­sti­tu­tions turn slowly[[x4]], Ajay Shah said, like a bat­tle­ship or a super tanker. The Western way of war learns through in­tro­spec­tion: di­aries, logs and books. {004-C12}

brief.head: A book for businessmen
brief.text: Tirthankar Roy’s *A Business History of India*[[x5]] showed Ajay Shah how lit­tle has changed. He urged even a busi­nessper­son who has never read a book to read it. {004-R15}

lead.kicker: Ajay Shah on OPEC, Amit Varma on guerrillas and Kashmir
lead.head: Big stick, short reach

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 4

body: Ajay Shah brought a car­tel that never quite ruled the oil mar­ket. Amit Varma brought armies that keep los­ing to guer­ril­las, and an ar­gu­ment that India keeps get­ting it wrong.
## Seven times in fifty years

OPEC, Shah said, was the car­i­ca­ture of a car­tel: at its peak, all the world’s oil pro­duc­ers agree­ing to fix a price and cut sup­ply, and, as gov­ern­ments, be­yond the reach of any an­titrust law.
Yet crude cost about $11 a bar­rel in 1974 and about $77 in 2023. That is roughly seven times, he said, or about 1.5 per cent a year in real terms. {004-S01}
“You tell me that you’ve got this pow­er­ful car­tel that’s con­trol­ling the price,” Shah said, “and all they’ve man­aged to get is about one and a half per cent real of a price hike.”

He gave three rea­sons. In the short run de­mand barely moves, be­cause you still have to drive to work. In the long run peo­ple ad­just dra­mat­i­cally, find­ing new oil, thriftier cars and sub­sti­tutes.

Second, no­body likes to be ex­torted. If India made its call cen­tres refuse to work for JP Morgan, Shah said, the bank would suf­fer for three weeks, and then the world would learn to man­age with­out India.
“In a con­flict the other guy gets a vote,” he said. {004-C03}
Third, car­tels leak. Thinly pop­u­lated Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Qatar could af­ford to cut out­put, while Iran and Iraq, with large pop­u­la­tions, kept sell­ing.
## The buyers’ turn

Then the story ran back­wards. After Russia in­vaded Ukraine, its crude went mainly to India and China, and the West capped the price at $60 a bar­rel by lean­ing on Western ship­ping and in­sur­ance firms.
Putin needed money for the war and had only two buy­ers left. “So sud­denly, in­stead of OPEC being a car­tel of sell­ers, you had China and India as a car­tel of buy­ers,” Shah said. {004-S02}
## Winning the peo­ple
Varma’s rab­bit hole began with a sec­ond­hand book in a Bangalore shop and led to David Galula’s 1960s clas­sic on coun­terin­sur­gency.
“If a fly and a lion are fight­ing, the fly can­not de­liver a knock­out blow, and the lion can­not fly,” Varma said, bor­row­ing Galula’s metaphor. {004-C06}

One of Mao’s gen­er­als put it as 20 per cent mil­i­tary and 80 per cent po­lit­i­cal. India in Kashmir, Varma ar­gued, was more or less 100 per cent mil­i­tary, and alien­ated the peo­ple it calls its own.

If Kashmir is an in­te­gral part of India, he said, Kashmiris are Indian cit­i­zens, and the state’s job is to serve them, not rule over them. He ap­plied Mancur Olson’s rov­ing and sta­tion­ary ban­dits to the Naxal areas in the same spirit.

Shah turned David Petraeus’s test, whether an op­er­a­tion takes more bad guys off the street than it cre­ates, into the arith­metic of epi­demics. If killing one mil­i­tant cre­ates 1.01 more on av­er­age, he said, “then you’ve had it be­cause this thing will ex­plode”. {004-C07}
He also warned against the se­cu­ri­ti­sa­tion of the state, in which in­vok­ing na­tional se­cu­rity brings all ques­tions to a stop.

The episode ended with books, films and a bet. Shah rec­om­mended Tirthankar Roy’s *A Business History of India*; Varma called Krzysztof Kieślowski’s *Dekalog* the pin­na­cle of cin­e­matic sto­ry­telling.

Then a re­mark about stock in­dexes for vices set off Varma, a pro­fes­sional poker player for five years. Everything in life is a gam­ble, he said, watch­ing this show in­cluded: “So well done, you’re a gam­bler.”

second.label: Kashmir
second.head: The year Kashmir hoped
second.deck: Amit Varma, drawing on David Devadas, on a chance India let slip

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Kashmir’s lost moment of 2007

body: Kashmir had a chance in 2007, Amit Varma said. Drawing on David Devadas’s *The Generation of Rage in Kashmir*, he de­scribed a new gen­er­a­tion sick of fight­ing, want­ing to be pro­gram­mers, en­gi­neers and artists. {004-R07}

But the se­cu­rity forces were en­trenched, and men who had fought on the front lines in the 1990s now held se­nior po­si­tions. Rewards for count­ing heads got in­no­cent peo­ple killed, and the need for per­mis­sion for ev­ery­thing bred rent-seeking and ex­tor­tion.

One young man re­fused to hand his Tata Indigo to a se­cu­rity man and was im­pris­oned. The win­dow closed, Pakistan came in, and things went to hell. It is hard, Varma said, not to ask how you would react in a Kashmiri boy’s shoes. {004-S04}

quote.text: You’ve seen your older brother taken away by the se­cu­rity forces and he dis­ap­pears.

third.head: Doom forgot the price tag

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the word the doomsayers forgot

body: The 1972 Club of Rome re­port fore­cast doom by me­chan­i­cally ex­trap­o­lat­ing con­sump­tion, Ajay Shah said. “And what was miss­ing in that en­tire think­ing was the word price.” {004-C04}

Amit Varma called peak oil a crack­pot con­spir­acy the­ory. {#peakoil} Scarcity raises prices, he said, and higher prices spur ex­plo­ration, re­new­ables[[x1]] and per­haps nu­clear: “We re­spond to in­cen­tives.”

Shah added that lithium is not rare at all, being made in large amounts in the fur­nace of the stars. Serious peo­ple, he said, once drew up busi­ness plans to tow re­source-rich as­ter­oids back to Earth[[x2]]. {#asteroid}

Varma promptly pitched a Bollywood film: Akshay Kumar flies to an as­ter­oid made of lithium. Shah ob­jected that lithium is plen­ti­ful on Earth, and sug­gested tan­ta­lum, a name he had picked off the pe­ri­odic table. {004-J04}

p2.deck: Ajay Shah on a cartel that could not hold, Amit Varma on wars that force alone cannot win

quote.text: In the long run, how­ever, human be­ings ad­just dra­mat­i­cally.

box.title: Adam Smith’s suspicion
box.text: Adam Smith warned, as Ajay Shah para­phrased him, that men of the same pro­fes­sion sel­dom get to­gether with­out try­ing to rig the price. That is our men­tal model of car­tels, Shah said, and OPEC put it to the test. {004-J08}

sections.label: The sellers
sections.head: A cartoon of a cartel
sections.caption: OPEC’s fifty years of oil prices
body: OPEC, Ajay Shah said, was the car­i­ca­ture of a car­tel. At its peak it was a coali­tion of all the world’s oil pro­duc­ers, agree­ing to fix a price and to cut sup­ply to reach it. Because its mem­bers were gov­ern­ments, not firms, no an­titrust law could touch it.
Then he looked at the data. Crude was about $11 a bar­rel in 1974 and about $77 now: seven times, but only about 1.5 per cent a year in real terms. {004-S01}
## Three leaks in the pipe

The first was time. Price elas­tic­i­ties are low in the short term, he said: dou­ble the price and you still drive to work. But the higher price paid for ex­plo­ration on a large scale, and for cars that burn less fuel. {004-C02}

The sec­ond was ex­tor­tion. China tried to choke rare earths to Japan in 2012; Russia tried to choke Europe’s en­ergy. Victims an­swer such hard power by cut­ting their ex­po­sure, and gov­ern­ments ev­ery­where found ways to de-risk their economies from OPEC. {004-C03}

The third was cheat­ing. Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Qatar have small pop­u­la­tions and vast oil rev­enues, so they could cut sup­ply and wait. Iraq and Iran, with large pop­u­la­tions, were keen to sell more.

~ So when Saudi Arabia pulled back one to three mil­lion bar­rels a day, Shah said, oth­ers made it up, from the North Sea to Russia and Mexico. The cartel’s loud prom­ises at its meet­ings would not re­ally work out once mem­bers went home.

quote.text: In the long run, how­ever, human be­ings ad­just dra­mat­i­cally.

sections.label: The buyers
sections.head: A cartel of two customers
sections.caption: the reverse OPEC
body: The most in­ter­est­ing pe­riod, Ajay Shah said, is the re­cent one. When the war in Ukraine began in February 2022, Putin’s im­plicit threat was that Europe would shiver in its homes through the win­ter. Europe called the bluff[[x6]] and found an array of so­lu­tions.
Russian crude went mainly to India and China in­stead. “India is at about 51% of Russian crude oil sales,” Shah said. {#fiftyone}

Then the West in­vented a new tool of eco­nomic state­craft: a cap of $60 a bar­rel on all Russian crude sales. {#sixty} It could be en­forced be­cause al­most all the world’s ship­ping and ship­ping in­sur­ance is run out of Western coun­tries, most no­tably the UK.
## Full cir­cle

Shah doubted it would work: new tanker fleets would spring up[[x7]], and the *Financial Times* re­ported one op­er­at­ing out of Bombay. But the data sug­gest Russian sales were choked at $60. With a war to fund and only two buy­ers left, Putin faced a car­tel of cus­tomers who could drive a hard bar­gain. {004-S02}

~ The oil age it­self, Shah said, may end as the Saudi oil min­is­ter Ahmed Zaki Yamani pre­dicted, through tech­nol­ogy, now that Europe is set on de­car­bon­i­sa­tion. {004-J09} Siberian gas may still sit in the ground a thou­sand years from now.

quote.text: Almost all the ship­ping of the world and al­most all the ship­ping in­sur­ance of the world is run out of Western coun­tries

art.caption: Ajay Shah (left) on the reverse OPEC, with Amit Varma

sections.label: The insurgents
sections.head: Soup with a knife
sections.caption: the counterinsurgency canon
body: Amit Varma’s rab­bit hole, which began with Fred Kaplan’s *The Insurgents*, led to what he called the Bible of the lit­er­a­ture: David Galula’s *Counterinsurgency Warfare*. Galula, who had fought in China and Algeria, was once im­pris­oned by Mao’s men. {#galula}

His point was that fight­ing in­sur­gents is very dif­fer­ent from fight­ing a con­ven­tional war. Use con­ven­tional tac­tics, Varma said, and it is like using a fly swat­ter: the flies keep com­ing. {004-C06}
Kaplan sums up the method: push the in­sur­gents out, hold the area, win the people’s trust, re­place the insurgents’ po­lit­i­cal or­gan­i­sa­tion, then mop up.
## The miss­ing 80 per cent

One of Mao’s gen­er­als said coun­terin­sur­gency is 20 per cent mil­i­tary and 80 per cent po­lit­i­cal. {004-C05} T. E. Lawrence, in *Seven Pillars of Wisdom*, likened it to eat­ing soup with a knife. India in Kashmir, Varma said, was more or less 100 per cent mil­i­tary.
He was not ar­gu­ing against fight­ing ter­ror­ists from Pakistan or de­fend­ing bor­ders. But a state that claims a peo­ple as its own, he said, must serve them rather than rule them.

~ He saw the Naxal areas through Mancur Olson’s ban­dits. A rov­ing ban­dit robs a vil­lage and leaves; a sta­tion­ary ban­dit stays to tax it, so he builds in­fra­struc­ture. {004-C08} Where the state was ab­sent, both it and the Naxalites be­haved like rov­ing ban­dits.

quote.text: Will this op­er­a­tion take more bad guys off the street than it cre­ates by the way it’s con­ducted?
quote.who: David Petraeus, as quoted by Amit Varma

sections.label: Shah’s reply
sections.head: Too important for generals
sections.caption: the securitised state
body: Ajay Shah heard in David Petraeus’s ques­tion the math­e­mat­ics that COVID taught ev­ery­one. If one in­fected per­son in­fects more than one other, an epi­demic ex­plodes; if killing one mil­i­tant cre­ates 1.01 new ones on av­er­age, so does an in­sur­gency. {004-C07}
He was also deeply un­com­fort­able with turn­ing the mil­i­tary, an in­sti­tu­tion de­signed for over­whelm­ing vi­o­lence, on India’s own pop­u­la­tion. {004-C10}
## When fear ends the ar­gu­ment

Then there is what he called the se­cu­ri­ti­sa­tion of the Indian state. Once na­tional se­cu­rity is in­voked, all ques­tions are sup­posed to stop. Emphasising fear, he said, is the surest way to wrong poli­cies, just as harp­ing on crises is a poor guide to fi­nan­cial pol­icy. {004-C11}

The French in Algeria and the Americans in Vietnam, Iraq and Afghanistan, Shah said, changed their con­duct through de­bate and crit­i­cism, and through in­tel­lec­tu­als like Petraeus. India lacks that ca­pac­ity, and not only in se­cu­rity: his book with Vijay Kelkar ar­gues that the state’s fail­ures cut across do­mains.

~ Amit Varma wor­ried that any army is an anachro­nism in fast-moving times. Shah replied that large in­sti­tu­tions ev­ery­where change slowly, and that climb­ing past lower-middle in­come needs a cul­ture of ev­i­dence, post-mortems and crit­i­cism. {#middleincome}

quote.text: War is too im­por­tant to be left to the gen­er­als, and se­cu­rity is too im­por­tant to be left to se­cu­rity peo­ple.

art.caption: Amit Varma (right) on the securitised state, with Ajay Shah

sections.label: The parting rant
sections.head: All of life at the tables
sections.caption: life as one long gamble
body: A stray mem­ory closed the episode. Ajay Shah re­called an index, he thought from Bloomberg, built from listed com­pa­nies that profit from each vice, gam­bling among them. {#vice}

Amit Varma, who was a pro­fes­sional poker player for five years, had a mini rant ready. {#poker} Poker is a game of skill[[x9]], he said, and not pure gam­bling. But ev­ery­thing we do is a gam­ble[[x8]].

Gambling, he said, is suss­ing up the prob­a­bil­i­ties and mak­ing a bet. A roulette wheel qual­i­fies, but so does talk­ing to a pretty woman in a bar, buy­ing a house ru­moured to be haunted be­cause it is cheaper, or launch­ing this show. {004-C14}
## Mistakes and free­doms

Shah, who has never gam­bled, agreed that ex­pos­ing our­selves to risk is part of life. But lot­ter­ies, where you lose on av­er­age be­cause the house al­ways wins, and de­riv­a­tives po­si­tions that burn through a bal­ance sheet, were to him de­ci­sion mis­takes. {#lottery}

Varma an­swered that it is up to the in­di­vid­ual to make those mis­takes, and the state should not get in­volved. When Shah called lot­ter­ies a tax on the dumb, Varma asked who is to de­cide who is dumb.
~ He signed off the same way: any­one still watch­ing had gam­bled on the show, and en­joyed it. {004-J07}

quote.text: Everything we do in our lives is gam­bling be­cause after all, what is gam­bling?
If you’re say­ing Kashmir is an in­te­gral part of India, I strongly be­lieve that that means that Kashmiri peo­ple are Indian peo­ple, you have to treat them like your own cit­i­zens.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: A cartel’s birth, a bookshop quarrel and two films that stayed with Varma

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on how OPEC was born, and what it achieved
stories.head: Born in anger, beaten by time
body: Before 1973, Ajay Shah said, there had been a long and easy col­lab­o­ra­tion be­tween the Arab oil pro­duc­ers, most no­tably Saudi Arabia, and the Western con­sumers of crude. It was live and let live, and OPEC had not yet found its feet.

Then came the 1973 war.[[x11]] The Arab coun­tries had lost to Israel in 1967 and pre­pared for a re­match. They got their strate­gic sur­prise, but Israel picked it­self up and won again, and the Arab street, Shah said, was left with hu­mil­i­a­tion, frus­tra­tion and blind­ing ha­tred.

In that fit of anger, a group of oil-producing coun­tries de­cided to raise the price of crude[[x10]]. They cut pro­duc­tion by only 8 per cent, and the price went from about $1.5 a bar­rel to $11. {#cut8}

Later his­to­ries show that the pro­duc­ers them­selves thought it reck­less. Some pow­er­ful oil-consuming coun­try, they feared, might sim­ply land an army and grab the oil fields of the Persian Gulf.
Henry Kissinger, it is be­lieved, wrote a pseudony­mous mag­a­zine ar­ti­cle set­ting out such an op­er­a­tion in de­tail, to turn the Gulf’s oil-producing re­gions into a global trust. {#kissinger}
No army came. “And sud­denly the Arabs looked at each other say­ing, Wow, we got such a big in­crease in the oil price,” Shah said. The car­toon car­tel was born.
~ Then he ran the num­bers. Crude went from about $11 in 1974 to about $77 in 2023, and that, he said, is about 1.5 per cent a year in real terms over “the suc­ceed­ing 53 years”. {004-S01}
stories.why: A price shock can look like proof of a cartel’s power, but it is often the short run talk­ing. Given time, de­mand ad­justs, vic­tims route around ex­tor­tion, and mem­bers with dif­fer­ent needs cheat on one an­other. {004-C02}
stories.postscript: Fifty years later the story ran in re­verse: after the 2022 war, India and China be­came a car­tel of buy­ers. {004-S02}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the birth of the oil cartel

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a father, a son and a frozen lake
stories.head: Within the margin of error
body: Krzysztof Kieślowski, the Polish film­maker, was com­mis­sioned by Polish tele­vi­sion to make ten short films on the Ten Commandments. {#tenfilms} Amit Varma calls the se­ries, *Dekalog*, the pin­na­cle of cin­e­matic sto­ry­telling.

The first film takes the com­mand­ment “Thou shalt not have any other god than me”. Its hero is a sci­en­tist, “very much like you”, Varma told Ajay Shah. The man’s young son is wait­ing for the lake to freeze so that he can go skat­ing.

The fa­ther mon­i­tors the tem­per­a­ture every day, and the weather re­ports, and ev­ery­thing else. At last he con­cludes that today, within the mar­gin of error, it is safe. The boy goes skat­ing. The ice cracks, and he dies. {004-S05}
~ In the last shot the fa­ther stands by the lake. In the dis­tance a home­less man has lit a fire to warm his hands.

quote.text: This film doesn’t have an anti-science mes­sage to me. Instead, it has an im­por­tant hu­mil­ity mes­sage to me.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the father who calculated the ice

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a scene he uses to teach writing
stories.head: Round and round in sheer joy
body: Two of the *Dekalog* films were made into longer films, and Amit Varma calls both mas­ter­pieces. {004-R17} In *A Short Film About Love*, a young man in an apart­ment com­plex has a crush on a woman across the way, and creep­ily spies on her through her win­dow.
One day he de­cides to go up to her door, per­haps while de­liv­er­ing the milk or the pa­pers, and ask her out. He rings the bell.

A stereo­typ­i­cal film, Varma said, would show the door open­ing, the ques­tion and her an­swer. Kieślowski cuts in­stead to a top-angle shot of the court­yard below, where the young man rides round and round on a cycle in sheer joy. {004-S06}
~ “And it just tells you ev­ery­thing,” Varma said. He uses the scene to teach his writ­ing stu­dents.
stories.why: Show, don’t tell works even in cin­ema[[x12]], Varma said. Kieślowski skips the ob­vi­ous beats, the door, the ques­tion, the an­swer, and trusts one image of a young man on a bi­cy­cle to carry the emo­tion.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the boy on the bicycle

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on Church Street and the rival bookshop
stories.head: One copy too many
body: When Amit Varma goes to Bangalore, he stays on Church Street, home to the stu­dio where he records, a Starbucks and Blossoms, his favourite book­shop in the world[[x13]].

Once he recorded an episode of *The Seen and the Unseen* with Ram Guha. {#guha} When Varma said he was off to the best book­shop in the world, Guha, in Varma’s ad­mit­tedly em­bel­lished retelling, called him a fool: Blossoms was not even the best on Church Street.

Guha’s pick was Bookworm. Varma vis­ited both. “It turned out Bookworm ac­tu­ally had a copy of a shitty book I wrote a decade and a half ago,” he said. “So I im­me­di­ately con­cluded Blossoms is bet­ter.” {004-S03}
~ Later, in Blossoms’ sec­ond­hand sec­tion, he found Fred Kaplan’s *The Insurgents* on sale. It began this episode’s rab­bit hole. {004-R03}
stories.why: One chance find can open a whole field. For Varma, a book like Kaplan’s be­comes an entry into a uni­verse: he will then read 30 other books, going down rab­bit hole after rab­bit hole[[x14]].
stories.postscript: If you go to Bali for a week, Varma said, he will go for a week to Blossoms. {004-J05}

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 4. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Krzysztof Kieślowski (Alberto Terrile, CC BY-SA 3.0); Adam Smith (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Vladimir Putin (Пресс-служба Президента России, CC BY 4.0); T. E. Lawrence (Harris & Ewing, public domain); David Petraeus (Darren Livingston, public domain). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon and Wikipedia.

shelf.title: The Wealth of Nations
shelf.creator: Adam Smith
shelf.why: The found­ing text on how na­tions be­come pros­per­ous: Ajay says Smith is to eco­nom­ics what Darwin is to bi­ol­ogy, and it is ‘eerie’ how much he got right.

shelf.title: A Deep Dive Into Ukraine vs Russia (Episode 335 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah
shelf.why: A five-and-a-half-hour mas­ter­class from Ajay on the war and the deep his­to­ries of Russia and Ukraine, built on a life­time of read­ing and a counter to Russian pro­pa­ganda.

shelf.title: The Insurgents
shelf.creator: Fred Kaplan
shelf.why: It is a re­cent book that cov­ers Petraeus and later de­vel­op­ments in coun­terin­sur­gency think­ing.

shelf.title: Counterinsurgency Warfare: Theory and Practice
shelf.creator: David Galula
shelf.why: Its cen­tral point is that fight­ing in­sur­gents is com­pletely dif­fer­ent from con­ven­tional war, cap­tured in the fly-versus-lion metaphor and the prin­ci­ple that you must keep the peo­ple on your side.

shelf.title: Seven Pillars of Wisdom
shelf.creator: T. E. Lawrence
shelf.why: It is part of the early lit­er­a­ture on guer­rilla war that ex­isted long be­fore the US went into Vietnam and still failed to learn from it.

shelf.title: Learning to Eat Soup with a Knife
shelf.creator: John Nagl
shelf.why: It sits in the coun­terin­sur­gency canon Amit worked through after Kaplan and Galula, which con­vinced him that this kind of war is mostly a po­lit­i­cal prob­lem.

shelf.title: The Generation of Rage in Kashmir
shelf.creator: David Devadas
shelf.why: Devadas ar­gues that 2007 was a mo­ment of hope, with a new gen­er­a­tion that wanted jobs and nor­mal lives.

shelf.title: The Seen and the Unseen episode with Srinath Raghavan
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Srinath Raghavan
shelf.why: Srinath Raghavan on India-Pakistan re­la­tions and, in great de­tail, the his­tory of the Kashmir prob­lem; Amit cites it for the view that the nu­clear shadow doesn’t make con­ven­tional war go away.

shelf.title: India, Pakistan, Kashmir: We Won’t Need To Fight A War If We Can Win The Peace
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: It sets out his ar­gu­ment that India treated Kashmir as a purely mil­i­tary prob­lem and lost its peo­ple, when the job of the state is to serve its cit­i­zens rather than rule over them.

shelf.title: A Tale Of Two Bandits: Naxals And The Indian State
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: It ap­plies Mancur Olson’s rov­ing-versus-stationary-bandit frame to India’s Naxal areas.

shelf.title: The Logic of Collective Action
shelf.creator: Mancur Olson
shelf.why: Olson’s ac­count of ‘con­cen­trated ben­e­fits and dif­fuse costs’: why small, or­gan­ised in­ter­est groups beat the large, un­or­gan­ised pub­lic.

shelf.title: The Indian Armed Forces (Episode 175 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Lt Gen Prakash Menon
shelf.why: An ear­lier deep con­ver­sa­tion about the Indian Army with Lt Gen Prakash Menon, who gives the army’s side on Kashmir: what is it sup­posed to do if Pakistan sends its peo­ple in?

shelf.title: The Liberal Nationalism of Nitin Pai (Episode 318 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Nitin Pai
shelf.why: A long-form de­bate in which Nitin Pai, whom both hosts ad­mire, de­fends ‘lib­eral nationalism’ and Amit ar­gues against it, on the ten­sion be­tween de­fend­ing a nation’s bor­ders and serv­ing its peo­ple.

shelf.title: In Service of the Republic
shelf.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ frame­work for Indian eco­nomic pol­icy: when the state should step in, why its fail­ures cut across every do­main (HR, con­tract­ing, bud­get­ing, checks on co­er­cive power), and why the fix is checks and bal­ances and small, re­versible steps.

shelf.title: A Business History of India
shelf.creator: Tirthankar Roy
shelf.why: It tells the story of India’s evo­lu­tion through the lens of firms and mar­kets.

shelf.title: Dekalog
shelf.creator: Krzysztof Kieślowski
shelf.why: Ten films made for Polish tele­vi­sion, ‘a web se­ries be­fore the web’, which Amit calls the pin­na­cle of cin­e­matic sto­ry­telling, above even Kieślowski’s Three Colours tril­ogy.

shelf.title: A Short Film About Killing
shelf.creator: Krzysztof Kieślowski
shelf.why: Amit names it along­side A Short Film About Love, and calls both of them mas­ter­pieces.

laughs.text: On whether the Saudi oil min­is­ter was imag­in­ing nu­clear fu­sion re­plac­ing oil, Ajay notes that fu­sion ‘is al­ways the great tech­nol­ogy of the next 20 years and has al­ways been and will al­ways be.’
Amit re­calls Ajay’s ear­lier joke that Putin de­serves a Nobel Prize for solv­ing cli­mate change, since his war set off a rush of European in­vest­ment in re­new­ables.

Amit pitches a Bollywood film: Akshay Kumar flies a space­ship to an as­ter­oid made of lithium and brings it back. Ajay ob­jects that lithium is plen­ti­ful on Earth, so you’d need a heavy el­e­ment. Tantalum gets sug­gested, and Ajay ad­mits he just picked a name off the pe­ri­odic table, which has ‘all kinds of beau­ti­ful names’ like yt­trium.
Amit on his love for Blossoms’ sec­ond­hand sec­tion: ‘if you want to go for a week to Bali, I’ll go for a week to Blossoms.’
In the gam­bling de­bate, Ajay says ‘Lotteries are a tax on dumb peo­ple.’ Amit replies: ‘I would argue for the au­ton­omy of dumb peo­ple... who’s to de­cide who is dumb and who is not?’
Amit’s sign-off: ‘It’s been a gam­ble on your part to watch it, and if you’re still here, you’ve en­joyed it, right? So well done, you’re a gam­bler.’

Adam Smith, as Ajay para­phrases him: ‘men of the same pro­fes­sion sel­dom get to­gether in the same room with­out try­ing to rig the price.’ Ajay uses it to state the stan­dard men­tal model of car­tels be­fore show­ing how OPEC fell short of it.

Saudi oil min­is­ter Ahmed Zaki Yamani: ‘the Stone Age did not end be­cause the world ran out of stones.’ The oil age will end through tech­no­log­i­cal change, which Ajay says is now hap­pen­ing through de­car­bon­i­sa­tion. He adds that Siberian gas may still be sit­ting in the ground a thou­sand years from now.

Henry Kissinger is be­lieved to have writ­ten a pseudony­mous mag­a­zine ar­ti­cle in the 1970s de­tail­ing a mil­i­tary op­er­a­tion to seize the Persian Gulf oil fields and turn them into a global trust. It re­flected a real fear among the OPEC pro­duc­ers them­selves.
Bob Dylan, ‘one of our heroes’: Amit quotes ‘A Hard Rain’s A-Gonna Fall’ as rain pours down out­side the record­ing.

Ajay re­calls Bloomberg build­ing stock mar­ket in­dexes for each vice, pick­ing listed com­pa­nies that profit from things like gam­bling. This is what set off Amit’s rant that all of life is gam­bling.
